subtopic_detail: Fluctuating inattention and withdrawal after hip surgery mistaken for low mood in an older patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked by the orthopaedic team to consider starting an antidepressant for an 84 year old woman on day three after a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. The team reports that she is withdrawn, tearful and not participating with physiotherapy.

Her daughter says that at home a fortnight ago she was managing her own finances and shopping independently, and that she has never been depressed. On assessment her attention fluctuates markedly within the interview, she cannot recite the months backwards, and she was reported by night staff to be drowsy by day and awake and muddled at 3 am. Her pulse is 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air and temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. She is on regular oxycodone and has not opened her bowels since surgery, and her bladder is palpable to the umbilicus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention within the interview, unable to recite months backwards, drowsy by day and awake overnight, bladder palpable to the umbilicus, no bowel motion since surgery
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), chest radiograph clear, urine not yet obtained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night for depression with low appetite and poor sleep, and review her mood in two weeks
options.rationale: Depression does not cause fluctuating attention or a reversed sleep wake cycle, and the two week horizon leaves reversible precipitants untreated. Hypoactive delirium is mistaken for depression more often than any other diagnosis in this setting. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain and a cognitive assessment for probable underlying dementia
options.rationale: Her daughter describes full independence a fortnight ago, which excludes an established dementia as the explanation for this change, and imaging without focal signs or a fall on the head has a very low yield. Cognitive assessment for dementia belongs after the acute episode has resolved. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard

options.text: Start regular low dose risperidone to settle the disturbed nights, and review her behaviour in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium or improve outcomes and are associated with increased mortality in older people, so they are reserved for severe distress or risk that persists after non pharmacological measures. She is withdrawn rather than agitated. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard

options.text: Start temazepam at night to restore her sleep pattern, and review her participation with physiotherapy in two days
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen and prolong delirium in older people except when the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal. Using one to normalise the sleep wake cycle addresses a symptom while deepening the confusion. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard

options.text: Treat the urinary retention and constipation, review the opioid, and institute non pharmacological supportive measures
options.rationale: Fluctuating attention with an altered sleep wake cycle days after major surgery in someone previously independent is delirium, and the treatment is to find and reverse the precipitants, here retention, constipation and opioid load. Non pharmacological measures including orientation, mobilisation, sensory aids and sleep hygiene are the evidence based core of management. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard

explanation.summary: Delirium affects up to half of older people after hip fracture surgery and is independently associated with longer stay, institutionalisation, persistent cognitive decline and death. It is defined by an acute onset, a fluctuating course, inattention, and disturbance of cognition or consciousness, and the hypoactive form, which is the commonest in older people, is routinely mislabelled as depression, fatigue or dementia because the patient is quiet rather than disruptive. An informant history establishing the premorbid baseline is the single most useful piece of information. Management is to identify and treat precipitants, with the usual culprits being pain, opioids and other deliriogenic drugs, constipation, urinary retention, infection, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and hypoxia, combined with non pharmacological measures such as reorientation, early mobilisation, restoring glasses and hearing aids, and protecting sleep. Antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress or risk and do not shorten the episode, and benzodiazepines are avoided unless the cause is withdrawal.
key_points: Hypoactive delirium is commonly mistaken for depression in older inpatients
Acute onset, fluctuation and inattention define the diagnosis
An informant history of the premorbid baseline is the key discriminator
Treat precipitants and use non pharmacological measures first
Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and benzodiazepines worsen it
explanation.pearls: Ask the family whether the person could manage their own money and medications a month ago, because a clear account of recent independence converts an apparently chronic confusion into an acute change requiring a search for precipitants, and that one question changes the management of more inpatients than any cognitive screening instrument.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium clinical care standard

subtopic_detail: Psychosis that outlasts the mood episode by several weeks in someone with recurrent mania
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman on an inpatient unit. Over her seven year history she has had three manic episodes and two depressive episodes, each with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations that were present only while her mood was disturbed.

During this admission her mania resolved five weeks ago and her mood has been euthymic on objective rating for four weeks, with normal sleep, normal energy and no grandiosity. She nevertheless continues to hear two voices commenting on her actions and remains convinced that staff are relaying information about her to a government agency. Her urine drug screen is negative on three occasions, her thyroid function and inflammatory markers are normal, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is unremarkable. She is adherent with her medication and has not taken corticosteroids.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood with normal sleep and energy, no pressure of speech, persistent third person auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on three occasions, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain unremarkable

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits her presentation?

options.text: Delusional disorder, persecutory type, given the fixed and circumscribed belief that staff are reporting on her
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires the absence of prominent hallucinations and of a mood disorder history, and she has both. Prominent auditory hallucinations alone exclude it. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, given the recurrent manic episodes that have dominated her seven year history
options.rationale: In that disorder psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during mood episodes and remit with them, which was her previous pattern but is no longer what is happening. The change in pattern is the finding that redirects the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Schizophrenia, given the persistent third person auditory hallucinations and systematised persecutory beliefs
options.rationale: Mood episodes have been present for the majority of her illness, which excludes this diagnosis, where mood symptoms are brief relative to the psychotic illness. The content of the hallucinations does not decide between the two. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, given psychosis persisting well beyond the resolution of the mood episode
options.rationale: The defining requirement is delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, with mood episodes present for the majority of the illness, and four weeks of euthymia with continuing psychosis meets it. The distinction is longitudinal rather than cross sectional. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder, given that stimulant use commonly produces persecutory beliefs of this kind
options.rationale: Three negative drug screens and psychosis persisting five weeks into an inpatient admission make ongoing substance exposure implausible. Substance induced psychosis characteristically settles within weeks of abstinence. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder sits between the mood and psychotic illnesses and is one of the least reliably applied diagnoses in psychiatry, largely because clinicians attempt to make it from a single cross sectional assessment. It requires two things: an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode occurs concurrently with the symptom criteria for schizophrenia, and delusions or hallucinations for two weeks or more in the absence of a major mood episode across the lifetime of the illness. Mood episodes must also be present for the majority of the total duration. The practical implication of that second criterion is that the diagnosis can only be made by charting mood and psychotic symptoms against each other over time, which is why a longitudinal chart or life chart is more useful than any single interview. Distinguishing it matters because management combines an antipsychotic with a mood stabiliser, prognosis is intermediate between bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, and clozapine is considered where psychosis remains resistant.
key_points: Requires psychosis for two weeks or more without a major mood episode
Mood episodes must be present for most of the total illness duration
Diagnosis is longitudinal and cannot be made from one assessment
Psychotic symptoms in bipolar disorder remit with the mood episode
Treatment combines an antipsychotic with a mood stabiliser
explanation.pearls: Build a life chart plotting mood episodes and psychotic symptoms on the same timeline with the patient and a family member, because the diagnosis turns entirely on whether the two lines separate, and this is the one piece of work that distinguishes it from bipolar disorder with psychotic features without requiring any further investigation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline
RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Falling phosphate on the third day of nutritional rehabilitation in a severely underweight patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar looking after a 19 year old woman admitted with anorexia nervosa at a body mass index of 12.8 kg/m2, having eaten very little for six weeks. Nasogastric feeding began three days ago under a joint medical and psychiatric plan.

Her phosphate has fallen from 1.12 mmol/L on admission to 0.52 mmol/L this morning, magnesium is 0.62 mmol/L and potassium is 3.1 mmol/L. She is mildly breathless with a pulse of 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air and temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius. Her jugular venous pressure is not raised, her chest is clear and there is trace ankle oedema. Thiamine was given before feeding started and continues daily. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 430 milliseconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 12.8 kg/m2, trace ankle oedema, chest clear, jugular venous pressure not raised, proximal weakness on sit to stand
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.52 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), electrocardiogram showing corrected QT interval 430 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the nasogastric feed entirely until the phosphate has normalised, then restart at the original rate
options.rationale: Withholding nutrition in a patient at this body mass index carries its own immediate mortality and simply defers the same problem to the restart. Underfeeding for fear of refeeding syndrome causes more harm in Australian units than the syndrome itself. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Replace phosphate orally alone and increase the feed rate as planned, since she is clinically stable on examination
options.rationale: A phosphate this low with breathlessness and proximal weakness indicates established refeeding syndrome, where oral replacement is too slow and increasing the rate accelerates the intracellular shift. Her apparent stability is exactly what precedes cardiac decompensation. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Replace phosphate intravenously, give a further loading dose of thiamine, and increase the feed rate as planned
options.rationale: Continued thiamine is correct and already being given, but it does not license increasing the calorie load while the electrolytes are falling. The rate is the variable driving the shift and must come down rather than up. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium intravenously and continue feeding at a reduced rate with daily electrolytes
options.rationale: Refeeding hypophosphataemia is treated by aggressive electrolyte replacement while nutrition continues, because stopping feeding prolongs starvation and its own mortality. Australian guidance is to slow rather than stop the rate and to monitor electrolytes at least daily through the first week. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Replace phosphate intravenously, start a loop diuretic for the oedema, and continue feeding at the planned rate
options.rationale: Refeeding oedema results from sodium and water retention as insulin rises and resolves with time, while a diuretic worsens the electrolyte depletion that is the actual danger. Diuresis in this setting is a recognised avoidable harm. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the metabolic consequence of reintroducing carbohydrate after prolonged starvation: insulin rises, glucose and electrolytes move into cells, and phosphate, potassium and magnesium fall abruptly while thiamine is consumed as a cofactor. The results are cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, haemolysis and Wernicke encephalopathy, typically in the first three to five days of feeding. The highest risk group includes a body mass index below 14 kg/m2, negligible intake for more than ten days, and pre existing electrolyte depletion. Prevention is thiamine before any carbohydrate, a cautious starting rate, and daily electrolyte measurement. When electrolytes fall, the modern approach is to replace aggressively and reduce the feeding rate rather than stopping, since the underfeeding syndrome that results from excessive caution is now recognised as the greater risk in specialist units. Cardiac monitoring is used where the corrected QT interval is prolonged or potassium is very low.
key_points: Insulin driven intracellular shift lowers phosphate, potassium and magnesium
Highest risk with body mass index below 14 kg/m2 and prolonged negligible intake
Give thiamine before any carbohydrate and continue it daily
Replace electrolytes aggressively and slow the feed rather than stopping it
Underfeeding from excessive caution causes more harm than the syndrome itself
explanation.pearls: Feed through the electrolyte disturbance rather than around it, and check phosphate, magnesium and potassium at least daily for the first week and twice daily if any is falling fast, because the nadir is usually on days three to five and a single daily sample can miss a rapid drop in a patient whose respiratory muscles are already weak.

sources.label: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Intrusive images of harming the baby that the mother finds abhorrent and acts to avoid
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the maternity ward to see a 29 year old woman five weeks after the birth of her first baby, referred urgently because she told the child health nurse she keeps imagining dropping the baby down the stairs.

She describes repeated unwanted images of the baby being harmed, which arrive unbidden many times a day and cause her intense distress and shame. She finds them abhorrent and has asked her partner to carry the baby up and down stairs and has stopped bathing the baby alone. She has no delusions, no hallucinations, no thought disorder and no elevated or irritable mood, sleeps when the baby sleeps, and her insight is fully preserved. She has never wanted to harm the baby and is frightened that admitting this will mean the baby is taken from her. She is breastfeeding and there is no substance use.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and tearful, fully oriented, no psychotic phenomena, insight preserved, appropriate attachment behaviour with the baby
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, ferritin 42 micrograms/L (15-200), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the nature of the symptoms, keep mother and baby together, and arrange cognitive behavioural therapy with a serotonergic antidepressant
options.rationale: Ego dystonic intrusive images with preserved insight and avoidance behaviour describe perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder, which carries no increased risk of harm to the infant and responds to exposure based cognitive behavioural therapy and a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor compatible with breastfeeding. Normalising the phenomenon is itself therapeutic because shame drives the concealment. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health

options.text: Make an immediate child protection notification and arrange supervised contact while the risk is formally assessed
options.rationale: Ego dystonic intrusive thoughts of this kind are not associated with increased risk of harm and are reported by the majority of new parents to some degree. A notification without a risk indicator is both unjustified and likely to deter her from disclosing anything further. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health

options.text: Arrange urgent admission to a psychiatric unit without the baby and start an antipsychotic for postpartum psychosis
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis presents with delusions, hallucinations, confusion or marked mood elevation and absent insight, and she has none of these. Separating a mother with obsessive symptoms from her infant reinforces the fear that keeps women silent about these thoughts. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health

options.text: Advise weaning so that a benzodiazepine can be started for her anxiety, with psychological therapy arranged afterwards
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat obsessive compulsive disorder and may reinforce avoidance, and weaning is unnecessary because effective treatments are compatible with breastfeeding. Advising a mother to stop feeding adds loss to an already distressing presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health

options.text: Provide reassurance alone and arrange general practice review in four weeks, treating this as a normal adjustment reaction
options.rationale: Intrusive thoughts are common in new parents, but hers occur many times daily with marked distress and avoidance that is restricting her care of the baby, which meets the threshold for a disorder. Reassurance without treatment leaves a treatable and often chronic condition to entrench. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health

explanation.summary: Intrusive thoughts of accidental or deliberate harm coming to the infant are reported by most new parents at some level, and become a disorder when they are frequent, distressing and drive avoidance or checking that interferes with care. Perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder affects roughly 2 to 4 percent of women after birth and is frequently concealed because mothers fear the consequences of disclosure. The clinical task is to distinguish it from postpartum psychosis, where the thoughts are ego syntonic, insight is impaired, and delusions, hallucinations, confusion or mood elevation are present, and where risk to the infant is genuinely increased and urgent admission to a mother and baby unit is indicated. The distinguishing features are whether the person finds the thoughts abhorrent and alien, whether insight is retained, and whether avoidance is being used to protect the baby, which is a protective rather than a risk behaviour. Treatment is exposure and response prevention with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, with sertraline the usual choice while breastfeeding.
key_points: Ego dystonic intrusive thoughts with preserved insight carry no increased risk of harm
Avoidance to protect the baby is a protective behaviour, not a warning sign
Postpartum psychosis involves delusions, confusion or mood elevation with impaired insight
Treatment is exposure based therapy with a serotonergic antidepressant
Sertraline is the usual antidepressant choice during breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether the thoughts feel like something she wants to do or something she is terrified of doing, because that single question separates the obsessional presentation from the psychotic one more reliably than the content of the thought itself, and mothers almost always answer it honestly once they are given the distinction.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period

subtopic_detail: Sequencing trauma focused work for a resettled refugee living with ongoing family separation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 38 year old man who arrived in Australia two years ago on a temporary protection visa after imprisonment and torture in his country of origin. He was referred by his general practitioner for headaches, back pain and insomnia for which no physical cause has been found.

Through an interpreter he describes nightmares most nights, being startled by doors closing, and avoiding the news. His wife and two children remain overseas in a camp and he has not been able to speak with them for two months. His visa is due for review in four months and he cannot work. He denies suicidal intent but says life feels pointless when he cannot protect his family. He drinks no alcohol, uses no drugs, and his physical examination and screening bloods are normal.

data_table.Examination: Guarded but engaged through an interpreter, low mood with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no current suicidal intent or plan
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin D 58 nmol/L (50-150), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Stabilisation with practical advocacy, sleep and pain management and psychoeducation, before starting trauma focused therapy
options.rationale: Trauma focused therapy requires a degree of present safety and stability, and his unresolved visa status and family separation represent ongoing rather than past threat, which predicts poorer tolerance and higher dropout. Australian refugee mental health services therefore begin with stabilisation and practical advocacy and introduce processing work once circumstances allow. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder

options.text: Refer him to a generic community mental health service and use a family member as interpreter to speed up assessment
options.rationale: Using family or community members as interpreters compromises confidentiality and accuracy and is particularly unsafe where torture is disclosed, and generic services rarely have the necessary expertise. Accredited interpreters and a specialist refugee service are the standard. (Source: Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma: Practice guidance)
source_refs: Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma: Practice guidance

options.text: Begin weekly trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy with imaginal exposure to the detention experiences immediately
options.rationale: Exposure work delivered while the threat is ongoing and the person has no secure base is associated with symptom exacerbation and disengagement. The therapy is right but the sequencing is wrong. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine for his insomnia and startle response, and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically not recommended in this condition because they impair the extinction learning that therapy depends on, carry dependence risk, and do not improve core symptoms. Insomnia here is better addressed behaviourally. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor alone and review in six weeks, deferring any psychological therapy
options.rationale: Medication has a place, particularly where symptoms are severe or therapy is not accessible, but it is second line to psychological treatment and does nothing about the practical circumstances driving his distress. Offering it alone frames a social and legal predicament as purely biochemical. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder

explanation.summary: Post traumatic stress disorder is common among people of refugee background, and Australian guidelines recommend trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first line treatment, with medication reserved for those who cannot access or do not respond to therapy. The complication in this population is that the threat is frequently ongoing rather than historical: insecure visa status, family separation, inability to work and fear of return all maintain hyperarousal and make processing work poorly tolerated. Somatic presentations such as headache, back pain and insomnia are also the common route into care, since psychological language for distress may be absent or stigmatised. The accepted approach is phased, beginning with safety, stabilisation, symptom management and practical advocacy including migration legal support and family tracing, and moving to trauma processing when circumstances permit. Accredited interpreters are used rather than family members, and specialist torture and trauma services exist in every Australian state.
key_points: Trauma focused therapy is first line, but sequencing depends on present safety
Ongoing visa insecurity and family separation are current threats, not past ones
Somatic complaints are a common presentation of this condition in this group
Benzodiazepines are not recommended and impair extinction learning
Use accredited interpreters and specialist torture and trauma services
explanation.pearls: Ask about the status of family members left behind and about the next visa decision date at every review, because these are usually the strongest predictors of symptom fluctuation in this group, and a deterioration in the weeks before a determination is a circumstantial response rather than a failure of treatment.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of acute stress disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder
Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma: Practice guidance
